opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's a really nice illustration of something that people often misunderstand about heritability. The intuition people have is that if a twin study tells you a trait is, say, 60 percent heritable, that's a fixed fact about human nature, as if the genes are doing 60 percent of the work and the environment is doing the other 40. But heritability isn't like that at all. It's a statistic about variation in a particular population in a particular environment.

So take smoking. Before there were restrictions, when cigarettes were cheap, everywhere, advertised, and socially normal, a lot of whether you smoked seemed to be predicted by genetic differences: how your body responds to nicotine, temperament, things like that. Then you introduce taxes, bans on smoking in public places, social stigma, and the picture changes. Now environmental factors, like whether you live somewhere with strict rules, what your peers do, what you can afford, carry much more of the weight, and the apparent genetic contribution shifts. Nothing about anyone's genes changed. What changed was the environment, and that changed how much genetic differences mattered for the outcome.

What I find so interesting is that it shows genes and environment aren't two separate pots you add together. They interact. The effect of a gene depends on the environment it's in, and the environment we're in is something we humans build. That's one of the distinctive things about us. We're constantly reshaping our own environments, and in doing so we change what our genes actually do.

It connects to something I care about in development. Children have a long childhood partly so they can adapt to whatever new environment they find themselves in, including environments their parents never imagined. So the idea that there's a fixed genetic destiny for behavior doesn't fit well with how flexible and culturally embedded human beings really are. Smoking is a vivid, concrete case where you can watch that happen in the data.

r001.rationale: The response says restrictions make environmental factors weigh more and the apparent genetic contribution shift, implying a smaller genetic contribution rather than a larger one.

r002.rationale: It does not explain that restrictions leave smokers with a stronger predisposition among those who continue smoking.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's one of the clearest illustrations of why heritability is not what people think it is. The intuitive picture is that there's some fixed number, the genetic contribution to smoking, and the environment is this separate thing that gets added on top. But what you actually see is that heritability estimates for smoking go up as the social restrictions on smoking go up. When smoking is everywhere, when everyone's doing it, when it's cheap and socially rewarded, the heritability is relatively low. And when you make it hard, when you ban it in restaurants and tax it and stigmatize it, suddenly the heritability goes up.

And when you think about it, that makes perfect sense. If everybody smokes, the differences between people aren't going to be driven by their genes, they're going to be driven by the fact that the whole culture is pushing them in one direction. Once you take that uniform pressure away, the people who are still smoking are the ones who have some strong internal pull toward it, whatever that turns out to be, and that's where the genetic variation shows up.

So the lesson is that heritability is always a statement about a particular population in a particular environment. It's not a measure of how biologically fixed something is. In fact, you can have a trait become more heritable precisely because the environment changed, which is just the opposite of what the folk picture would predict. And I think the same thing is true of the things I care about with children. When you change the environment, you don't just add or subtract from some genetic baseline, you change what the genes are doing and which differences get expressed at all. That's why I'm always skeptical when people take a heritability number and treat it as if it tells you what can or can't be changed.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly says smoking heritability estimates rise as social restrictions increase.

r002.rationale: It explains that under restrictions, those who continue smoking have a strong internal pull toward smoking, making genetic differences more apparent.

astra-6.text:
What’s interesting is that heritability depends on the environment. If smoking is something that everybody does because it’s socially accepted and cigarettes are readily available, then differences in genetic predisposition may not explain very much about who smokes. If you make smoking difficult and socially unacceptable, the people who still smoke may be disproportionately those with a strong genetic predisposition. So the apparent genetic contribution can go up even as smoking becomes much less common.

That’s a lovely illustration of why “heritable” doesn’t mean “unchangeable.” You could have an environmental intervention that dramatically reduces smoking and, at the same time, makes the remaining variation look more genetic.

r001.rationale: The response says that making smoking difficult and socially unacceptable can increase the apparent genetic contribution, even as smoking becomes less common; this answers the twin-study question in context.

r002.rationale: It explains that people who continue smoking under those restrictions may be disproportionately those with a strong genetic predisposition.
